title: Measuring concentration with light
summary: External standards and standard addition for ferricyanide analysis.
did: Prepared a five-point ferricyanide calibration series, collected absorbance measurements at 420 nm, and organized external-standard and standard-addition calculations in Excel.
why: Comparing calibration approaches helps explain how the sample matrix can influence an analytical measurement.
outcome: Produced lab reports, preparation calculations and worksheets that document the measurement process and provide a basis for comparing the two methods.
note: Analysis draft: calibration formulas and reported fit statistics need reconciliation with the measured data. No validated accuracy or concentration claim is made here.

title: Following an acid–base titration
summary: NaOH standardization and volumetric analysis of an unknown acid.
did: Used potassium hydrogen phthalate to standardize NaOH, collected my own titration measurements, and organized pH and volume data into worksheets and a written report.
why: Standardization connects the amount of titrant delivered to the amount of analyte, making concentration calculations meaningful.
outcome: Created an experimental record for examining titration behavior and evaluating the uncertainty in an unknown-acid analysis.
note: Analysis draft: reported titrant concentrations, equivalence points and stoichiometry are not fully consistent. The files are preserved as coursework, not as a validated identification of the unknown acid.

title: How precise is the preparation?
summary: A comparison of volumetric preparation methods using absorbance data.
did: Collected absorbance measurements for six preparation conditions with five measurements per condition, along with five blank measurements; organized blank correction and variability calculations in Excel.
why: Replicate measurements help distinguish the consistency of a preparation method from the size of a single reading.
outcome: Built a report and calculation workbook for comparing variation across preparation conditions and discussing measurement uncertainty.
note: Analysis draft: some spreadsheet references and uncertainty calculations require correction before numerical comparisons can be treated as final.

title: Tracking an indicator’s color change
summary: Spectrophotometric study of bromocresol green across buffer pH values.
did: Collected my own spectrophotometric measurements of bromocresol green in five buffers spanning pH 3.8–5.8 and organized the data for an acid–base equilibrium analysis.
why: An indicator’s changing absorbance connects a visible color change to the relative amounts of its acid and base forms.
outcome: Prepared a lab report and workbook connecting pH-dependent spectra with the method used to estimate an indicator’s pKa.
note: Analysis draft: wavelength labels, linked workbook calculations and the reported pKa require review. A verified pKa is not claimed.

title: Inorganic chemistry problem set
summary: Written chemistry coursework and worked subparts.
did: Organized worked responses to a CHEM 220 problem set in a single document.
why: Working through individual subparts makes chemical reasoning explicit and easier to review.
outcome: Created a structured coursework document that can be read alongside the laboratory projects.

title: A small course registration database
summary: A Python and SQLite system for students, courses and enrollments.
did: Implemented database tables and Python operations for registration, course lookup, enrollment, withdrawal and enrollment counts, using parameterized SQL queries and relational joins.
why: Separating students, courses and enrollments keeps the data organized and supports queries across related records.
outcome: Produced a working educational database project, notebooks and a final report using a small sample dataset to demonstrate the registration workflow.
note: Classroom prototype with sample data; not a deployed student-information system.
credit: The final report lists Duy Hoang and Leighanna Navales. Original report credits are retained.

title: Asking questions with SQL
summary: Database exercises involving queries and relational reasoning.
did: Wrote SQL and notebook-based solutions using filtering, joins and distinct results, and completed related relational-algebra exercises.
why: Translating a question into a query is a foundation for retrieving useful information from structured data.
outcome: Created a set of coursework examples that demonstrate how query structure changes the records returned.

title: Exploring a penny dataset
summary: An Excel workbook for descriptive statistics and distributions.
did: Organized a 281-row dataset containing year, mass and mint information, with summary statistics and distribution analysis.
why: Descriptive statistics reveal the spread and composition of a dataset before more complex analysis is attempted.
outcome: Produced a workbook that brings the observations and statistical summaries together for review.

title: From 3D coordinates to a 2D view
summary: A Toyota Corolla-inspired wireframe and transformation study.
did: Represented a model with 16 vertices and an adjacency matrix, then used Python, NumPy and Matplotlib to explore rotations, scaling and perspective projection.
why: Matrix transformations show how computer graphics translate geometric data into a view on a screen.
outcome: Implemented and documented five transformation cases, linking the mathematical operations with their plotted results.

resources.name: New Project Toyota Corolla Report Final.pdf

title: Inside a Linux kernel module
summary: A C timer module with a counter and a /proc interface.
did: Developed coursework in C using kernel timers, jiffies, logging and a /proc interface to expose a counter.
why: Kernel modules illustrate how low-level code interacts with the operating system beyond a normal user-space program.
outcome: Produced source files and a report documenting the timer and counter behavior as an educational systems project.
note: Educational source code; not a production driver. The portfolio does not execute kernel modules in the browser.

title: Coordinating five concurrent threads
summary: A POSIX threads exercise in shared-resource coordination.
did: Used mutexes, condition variables and state tracking to coordinate five threads and compare synchronized behavior with an unsynchronized approach.
why: Concurrency requires explicit coordination when multiple tasks compete for shared resources.
outcome: Created C source and a report that make the synchronization strategy and observed behavior available for inspection.
note: Coursework demonstration; no formal guarantee of freedom from deadlock or starvation is asserted.

title: Communicating through message queues
summary: A sender and receiver exercise using POSIX message queues.
did: Completed sender and receiver scaffolds to exchange messages, include process identifiers, handle a termination message and close and unlink the queue.
why: Message queues allow separate processes to communicate through an explicit interface.
outcome: Produced paired C programs demonstrating a simple interprocess communication lifecycle.
credit: Based on course-provided starter files; original comments are retained.

title: Signals, timers and module lifecycle
summary: Foundational Linux programming labs.
did: Worked with SIGALRM, sigaction and setitimer in a user-space timer exercise, and wrote a simple loadable module with initialization and exit functions.
why: These exercises connect event handling and program lifecycle to concrete operating-system interfaces.
outcome: Created commented C source and a lab write-up describing timer interrupts and module loading and unloading.

title: A closer look at Ruby
summary: A programming-language study with a report and presentations.
did: Researched Ruby’s language design, object model and dynamic behavior; assembled code examples, a written analysis and presentation materials.
why: Comparing language features helps explain how design choices affect readability and the way programs are written.
outcome: Produced a report and slide materials that communicate the language’s features and tradeoffs.
note: A language research project, not a deployed Ruby or Rails application.

title: Solving problems across languages
summary: Programming-language assignments and source-code exercises.
did: Completed exercises across Java, C#, C, C++, Racket and Prolog, with written work on language concepts and programming approaches.
why: Expressing problems in different languages exposes differences in control flow, data representation and reasoning.
outcome: Built a collection of assignment solutions and source files for comparing imperative, functional and logic-programming approaches.

title: Choosing an algorithm deliberately
summary: Written analysis of sorting algorithms and data structures.
did: Compared insertion sort and merge sort across input arrangements and discussed time complexity and data-structure choices.
why: Algorithm selection depends on input size, ordering and the costs of the operations a program performs.
outcome: Produced written comparisons that connect theoretical complexity to expected performance trends.
note: The portfolio presents written analysis; it does not claim independently reproduced benchmark improvements.

title: From Boolean expressions to assembly
summary: Computer-systems assignments and assembly exercises.
did: Worked through Boolean simplification and digital-logic exercises, alongside assembly examples covering arithmetic, comparisons and loops.
why: These topics connect high-level program behavior with lower-level representations and operations.
outcome: Assembled coursework and source examples showing the relationship between logic and machine-level instructions.

title: Reasoning about a Nash equilibrium
summary: A written game-theory assignment.
did: Completed a written analysis of strategic choices and Nash equilibrium.
why: Equilibrium reasoning examines how a participant’s best choice depends on the choices made by others.
outcome: Produced a coursework report that makes the reasoning available for review.

title: Understanding Linux access boundaries
summary: Controlled labs in permissions, environment variables and Set-UID behavior.
did: Configured users, groups and permissions in a lab, then investigated environment variables, process execution and Set-UID behavior.
why: Access controls and execution context determine which operations a process should be able to perform.
outcome: Documented lab observations and security implications in reports focused on least privilege and process boundaries.
note: All scenarios are classroom exercises; named organizations in the lab scenario are not employers or clients.

title: Investigating a buffer overflow
summary: A controlled SEED lab on memory safety and defenses.
did: Investigated buffer-overflow behavior in a Docker-based teaching environment and documented the roles of address randomization, stack protection and non-executable memory.
why: Memory-safety failures help explain why defensive controls are needed at both the code and platform levels.
outcome: Produced a report explaining the lab behavior and the purpose of the relevant protections.
note: Controlled academic lab, not a commercial penetration test.

title: Observing packets and filtering traffic
summary: Packet-analysis and firewall coursework in an isolated network lab.
did: Used Scapy to explore packet behavior and iptables rules to examine traffic filtering, forwarding and connection tracking in a Docker lab.
why: Packet inspection and explicit filtering rules help explain how network boundaries permit or deny traffic.
outcome: Created reports documenting the lab setup, rule behavior and observations for stateful and protocol-specific traffic controls.
note: Built on course-provided lab infrastructure. These are academic demonstrations rather than operational network deployments.

title: Testing web application defenses
summary: SQL injection and CSRF exercises in a local teaching environment.
did: Investigated SQL injection and cross-site request forgery in Docker-based PHP, MySQL and Elgg lab applications, and examined the behavior of CSRF token protections.
why: Separating user input from database commands and validating request intent are central to web application security.
outcome: Documented the lab attacks, observed behavior and relevant defenses in a report; prepared statements are discussed as a mitigation.
note: Controlled classroom applications only. Discussion of prepared statements does not imply a production remediation was implemented.
